entries.title: Dinner, Take 2
entries.content:
Today’s notice: White House reporters defend their big dinner. Maine Democrats hope for some stability. The speaker has had it. Russia sanctions stall. And: Democrats readying to take on the “anti-woke jobs board.”





THE LATEST

To redo or not to redo? It’s Washington’s most glamorous — and most controversial — night. Again. Donald Trump, most of his Cabinet and White House journalists are making a second attempt at the annual White House Correspondents’ Association dinner after a shooting halted April’s event.

This time, the dinner will be held at the Waldorf Astoria, formerly Trump International, even as the president derides reporters, sues news organizations and his White House keeps a list of “media offenders.” (The Justice Department dropped subpoenas against New York Times journalists yesterday, so they have that going for them.)

The perennial, and now more pertinent, question remains: Should journalists continue to host Nerd Prom? And what does it mean in the second age of Trump, when his administration is working harder than ever to find leakers and target reporters who break well-sourced stories?

Some 500 journalists and eight press organizations say the dinner should go. NOTUS’ Ben T.N. Mause and Manuela Silva surveyed White House reporters this week on whether there’s credibility to the argument that having the dinner is the same as honoring Trump. Many said canceling the event would be giving in.

“Some of the journalists he subpoenaed and has gone after verbally are going to be on stage with him receiving awards. I think that image, and celebrating a free press, will say more than boycotting the event would,” a White House reporter told us.

The contrary take: The dinners feed “into the narrative that D.C. journalists are elitist and out of touch with everyday Americans. ‘Look at them eating lobster, dressed in designer gowns and rubbing elbows with the very people they cover,’” another White House reporter said. That said, they added, don’t disinvite Trump — use the opportunity to call out his treatment of the media.

Open tabs: Number of U.S. troop deaths suddenly appears lower on Pentagon website (NYT); U.S. intelligence agency quietly cut about 200 jobs since June 1 (WaPo); Trump administration drops demands for list of Jewish employees at UPenn (Politico); Mortgage rates hit highest levels in nearly a year (WSJ); Oil surges to $100 per barrel after Red Sea attacks (NBC); Key Republican senator says he will support Trump’s pick for C.D.C director (NYT)





From the campaign trail


Southern swing: Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate, is headed south this weekend, campaigning for Senate candidate Annie Andrews in South Carolina and Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia, Murphy’s team shared exclusively with NOTUS’ Igor Bobic. His message? Democrats need to become a “big tent” party.

Hat trick: The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is on a 3x losing streak with high-profile losses that are causing House Democrats to question the campaign arm’s primary strategy.

Democrats want the DCCC to improve how it communicates with members and takes feedback, NOTUS’ Oriana González reports.

The Maine question: Democrats think they’ve stopped the bleeding in Maine’s Senate race with Troy Jackson as their heir apparent. “I think it’s going to be hotly contested, but I think it’s very much back in play,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico).

Jackson, the former state Senate president, has no federal political experience and only three months to assemble a campaign against a 30-year Republican incumbent, Sen. Susan Collins. But as his nomination becomes formal on Saturday, Democrats tell NOTUS’ Alex Roarty, Igor Bobic and Christa Dutton they think Jackson might be in a better position than Graham Platner was even before the sexual assault allegations.

From the Hill


Mike Johnson’s doom loop: After months of dealing with rebellions from members of his own party, the normally even-keeled speaker of the House had finally had enough and snapped, “I’m sick of this shit,” at Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Florida).

It was just one of a slew of daily crises Johnson has dealt with this year as members of his own conference threaten to derail their party’s agenda, NOTUS’ Reese Gorman reports. And rank-and-file Republicans are increasingly upset that a few of their colleagues hold so much power. Some are thinking of ways to actually hold the rebels to account.

“The Republican conference is a diverse gathering of people, some of whom are really effective at getting things done and others who are more interested in knocking things down,” Rep. Dusty Johnson (R-South Dakota) told Reese.

Still stalled: The long-championed (and long-stalled) bill by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham to enact more sanctions on Russia was poised to finally pass, boosted by the politician’s unexpected death. Instead, the measure is at risk of stalling out — again, NOTUS’ Igor Bobic and Joe Gould report.

“We’re going to screw around here and lose this bill if we don’t go vote,” Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) told our reporters. “We just pissed away two weeks. Now we got a week and a half left, and I don’t know if a vote is scheduled.”

From the White House


Thune v. Leavitt: Senate Majority Leader John Thune and White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt exchanged not-so-friendly fire yesterday over the SAVE America Act, the voter-ID bill Trump considers his top priority, NOTUS’ Al Weaver writes. Leavitt told reporters at a briefing that the president’s “patience was running out.” In turn, Thune shot back that “she or somebody else ought to get on the phone and get the votes, right?”





THE BIG ONE

The opposite of woke: A firm called RedBalloon, which claims to be the “anti-woke jobs board,” received a $1 million no-bid contract to help the State Department recruit candidates after the department laid off 20% of its workforce last year, NOTUS’ Eric Katz reports.

“A lot of the recruiting was focused on DEI. It was trying to get in the guy with a PhD in Black dance, rather than people who can do the best job,” Andrew Crapuchettes, the firm’s owner, said in a podcast interview recently. “I would love to see a lot of Christians applying, taking the test, doing the hard work, becoming a foreign service officer.”

Democrats, who say they want to help employees booted under a reduction in force get their jobs back, are planning to investigate if they retake power in Congress.

“We’re going to beef up our counsel staff so that we’re ready, because I can’t let folks get away with this,” Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-New York) told Eric.





NOTUS METRO

NOTUS has some of the best reporters covering D.C.-area news, sports and culture. Sign up for our local newsletter!

Sports desk: The Mystics Are Officially a Problem for the Rest of the WNBA, by Dave Sheinin





NEW ON NOTUS

McConnell’s absence impact: Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) has not voted since being hospitalized June 14, and his absence has complicated the math on some key Republican priorities, NOTUS’ Avani Kalra and Al Weaver report.

One example: The Senate Appropriations Committees is made up of 15 Republicans and 14 Democrats. Without McConnell, the committee cannot move any legislation forward that does not have bipartisan support.

More: House Republicans Focus on Democrats’ Plans, Not Their Own Wins, by Kadia Goba

Trump Expands His Ratepayer Pledge With Republican Governors, Utilities, by Mara Hoplamazian

Three Airports Opt Into Trump Administration’s New Private Airport Security Model, by Jenna Monnin

Trump Sidesteps SCOTUS With New Tariffs, by Violet Jira





NOT US

  • Marco Rubio Takes Aim at Globalists and the Left, by Ishaan Tharoor for The New Yorker
  • How Trump Is Getting Richer in Office, by Andrea Fuller, Daniel Wood and Ben Protess for The New York Times
  • Metro tried to make bus service better. Somehow, ridership and speeds are both down. By Rachel Weiner for The 51st

THE LATEST

South Carolina will be the first up to vote in the 2028 Democratic primary, the DNC Rules and Bylaws Committee voted today. The state’s 26 votes beat out Nevada (19) and New Hampshire (4).

entries.title: Trump Is Veering Toward Abandoning International Law
entries.summary: The “best” hope for de-escalation with Iran is that the president is “super distracted beautifying the District,” a source told NOTUS.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump wants to make a dramatic show of force against Iran — potentially one that implicates U.S. soldiers in war crimes under international law. And he has consistently been unwilling to back down during internal conversations, sources familiar with administration discussions said.

Combined with the Trump administration’s ongoing push to delegitimize the International Criminal Court, one of the global institutions meant to uphold standards for warfare, observers fear the U.S. is rapidly moving to abandon norms meant to shield human rights.

“It’s not the first time the U.S. has gone on a rampage to try and kill the court,” said Rebecca Hamilton, a former International Criminal Court lawyer, who noted that U.S. officials also tried to limit the body’s reach during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. “When they’re attacking the court like this, it raises the question of, Why are you so scared of this court?”

The U.S. has launched renewed strikes against Iran for 13 days in a row, and Trump threatened on Wednesday to destroy an Iranian bridge or power plant each time Iran strikes a ship attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz. Such an attack could have severe consequences for many civilians, who under international law countries are supposed to shield from military campaigns.

“The threat itself may violate [international law], and if U.S. forces actually carried through on the threat then yes, that would likely violate” the law, said Brian Finucane, a former State Department lawyer. He noted that rules around war bar indiscriminate attacks — those without clear military objectives — as well as threats against civilian objects or those intended to terrorize civilians.

Trump is showing signs of moving forward. Two sources familiar with administration thinking told NOTUS they expect a significant U.S. blitz against Iran in the coming days, motivated by Trump’s desire to look as though he is dominating Tehran. Neither source was authorized to speak on the record.

The “best” hope for de-escalation “is Trump is super distracted beautifying the District,” one source said, nodding to the president’s fixation on design choices around Washington. The likeliest outcome, they said: “pointless escalation.”

But the second source said many Cabinet members and military leaders have failed to be frank with Trump about the risks of launching his war on Iran in partnership with Israel, where officials have urged an assertive approach over diplomacy. Both sources expressed frustration with Brad Cooper, U.S. Central Command’s current chief, with one saying he could be the driving force behind added but likely futile American attacks.

U.S. Central Command did not respond to a NOTUS request for comment. Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, wrote in an email: “The United States signed [a memorandum of understanding] with Iran and they broke it, shot at commercial ships, and killed American soldiers. President Trump is not going to stand by and allow this terrorist behavior to occur. Iran is paying in massive bombs, night after night, and they will continue to pay until they come to the table in, what President Trump deems, a meaningful way.”

Experts on Iran say added U.S. military pressure has a low chance of securing the outcome Trump seeks: normal traffic through the strait for vital oil and gas shipments. Despite the U.S. signing an agreement with Iran in June that references Hormuz — among other disagreements between the two countries — and providing escorts and naval coordination for ships, energy flows remain low, with Iran arguing the U.S. is not respecting its claims to the strait. And now, the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen has warned it will close another major shipping route on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula, which could further damage the global economy. Trump has also threatened the Houthis in response.

Meanwhile, Secretary of State Marco Rubio has launched a campaign against the International Criminal Court, saying this month the body poses “an intolerable threat to U.S. sovereignty” and alleging it seeks to target Americans.

“There are certainly grounds for being very concerned” about the legal implications of Trump’s discussion of targeting Iranian infrastructure, said Hamilton, who is now a professor at American University.

The International Criminal Court, established by the Rome Statute in 2002, considers serious crimes and violations of international law that are not being fairly examined by domestic courts, serving as a court of last resort. U.S. officials were heavily involved in crafting the Rome Statute, but the country has never joined the court, despite previously supporting its investigations into figures including Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump has reportedly spoken of aligning with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to undermine the body.

Trump has also defended Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who judges at the International Criminal Court say should stand trial for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity over Israel’s U.S.-backed military offensive in Gaza. (Netanyahu has denied any criminality.)

The court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant, as well as a leader of the Palestinian militant group Hamas, in 2024. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said this month he would like to uphold the warrant and arrest Netanyahu if he visits the city for a United Nations summit in September, but lacks the legal ability to do so. Trump has retorted that Netanyahu will not be arrested if he comes to the U.S.

The U.S. and Iran aren’t members of the International Criminal Court, which limits its ability to probe either nation’s actions in this war. (Palestine is a member, which allowed the court to investigate Netanyahu and Gallant for actions on its territory.)

But 125 nations — most of the world’s countries — are members. With Rubio calling the court a threat to American sovereignty, Hamilton argued the U.S. should respect other states’ sovereign choices. On Friday, member states attempted to address a controversy that has plagued the court for more than a year by voting to remove its prosecutor, Karim Khan, over accusations of misconduct. Khan suggested he was targeted for his work on Gaza. For now, the warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant remain valid, though some worry a new prosecutor will downplay them, weakening the court’s work and the idea that some norms for behavior must be upheld.

Amid concerns about eroding international law, Mark Kersten, a professor at the University of Fraser Valley in Canada, said other nations could defend the court by increasing actions to uphold its warrants or allotting it more resources.

“The real story here is just how sensitive the United States is to the probability of being named in any kind of investigation” as its wars expand, he said.

entries.title: Trump Threatens the EU With Tariffs Over Fines on Tech Companies
entries.summary: The president accused the European Union of “illegal and highly discriminatory” practices against U.S. companies.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said Friday that the U.S. will launch an investigation into the European Union and potentially impose tariffs, claiming the bloc unfairly imposed billions of dollars in fines on the U.S.’s biggest tech companies.

“This illegal and highly discriminatory practice started at these high levels during the first year of the Sleepy Joe Biden Administration, but it’s not going to continue during the Trump Administration. The United States of America is not a ‘PIGGYBANK’ for Europe, nor will we allow it to be!” Trump wrote on Truth Social Friday, listing Apple, Meta, Amazon and Google as companies that have been excessively fined.

Trump said his administration will "immediately" launch an investigation under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The law allows for the imposition of tariffs if the investigation ends up providing evidence of unfair trade practices.

“The European Union will pay a very big price for this illegal and highly unethical conduct, which I have consistently warned them about,” Trump wrote in the post. “The penalties will be entirely reversed and, we anticipate, a substantial TARIFF to be placed on them at the earliest possible moment.”

The EU announced Thursday that it was fining Google the equivalent of $1 billion for what it said were breaches of antitrust rules through Google Play and its search engine.

The Trump administration condemned the fine later Thursday.

“The EU’s various fines of Google alone add up to over 2 percent of the EU’s budget—a larger 'contribution' to the budget than many EU member states. Add in the recent announcement of the largest ever state-backed loan to Airbus, and it becomes clear that the EU continues to target the most competitive U.S. companies,” Trade Ambassador Jamieson Greer said in a statement.

Trump faced a large setback to his tariff policy earlier this year when the Supreme Court decided in a 6-3 ruling to strike down the president’s sweeping tariffs on U.S. trade partners.

However, he’s found new ways to implement tariffs, including through Section 301 of the Trade Act. On Thursday, the U.S. imposed tariffs on 60 economies “for their failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor.”

entries.title: A Heritage Employee Was Caught With Drugs Trying to Get Into the Senate, Police Say
entries.summary: Matthew Christopher Wingate was stopped and searched for having a pistol magazine in his briefcase, according to a court affidavit.
entries.content:
A Heritage Foundation employee faces a drug-possession charge after a security screening at a Senate office building turned what tested presumptively positive as cocaine and fentanyl, according to court records.

Capitol Police officers detained Matthew Christopher Wingate on July 14 after he entered the Russell Senate Office Building and placed his bag on the X-ray belt as part of routine screening, according to an affidavit filed in Washington, D.C., superior court.

Wingate is the government-relations director for defense and foreign policy at the Heritage Foundation, and previously worked as a national security adviser for Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) and a military legislative assistant for Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), according to Legistorm.

An officer observed an image consistent with a pistol magazine inside the brown briefcase, and a secondary screening found a magazine with 10 rounds of 9 mm ammunition, the affidavit states.

Officers placed him under arrest, the affidavit states. That was apparently because of the magazine. Firearms and ammunition are generally prohibited from being carried into Senate office buildings.

Officers ran a check through the Metropolitan Police Department's Gun Registry Unit, which confirmed Wingate held a valid license to carry a firearm in D.C., the affidavit states.

A crime-scene officer discovered a plastic sandwich bag in the exterior pocket of the briefcase containing four capsules and three blue-pressed tablets, the affidavit states. Field testing of the blue pills, which were imprinted with the letter “A” on one side and “7 6” on the other side, returned a presumptive positive result for cocaine and fentanyl, the affidavit states.

Under questioning, Wingate said he forgot the magazine was in the briefcase and “explained that the drugs were his and were prescribed to him from a medical professional,” the affidavit states.

Wingate did not respond to multiple requests for comment. The Heritage Foundation and Wingate’s lawyer did not respond to requests for comment.

Wingate was released from custody on the misdemeanor charge and has an Aug. 27 court date, according to court records.

entries.title: Republicans Fret Trump Could Sink Mike Collins’ Georgia Senate Run
entries.summary: The president’s approval rating is underwater — could he bring down their candidate in one of the country’s most significant races?
entries.content:
Republicans are wary that a visible President Donald Trump in Georgia could do more harm than good as they try to win back Sen. Jon Ossoff’s seat.

Ossoff was widely seen as one of the most vulnerable Democrats up for reelection this year — particularly after Trump won the state in 2024. But with Mike Collins’ campaign already in a rut, they’re worried Trump's underwater approval rating in the state could further sink his chances.

“We're already seeing Ossoff at every turn trying to tie Collins to Trump,” a Republican operative, who requested anonymity due to his role on an active campaign, said. The operative added that when Trump’s approval rating sits below 40%, as it does now, “there's headwinds there.”

Collins’ general election campaign has struggled with scandal. One longtime staffer was fired after Collins' campaign account mocked a woman by referencing the fact that she said she was a victim of sexual assault; Collins called the post “despicable and unauthorized.” Another official aide reportedly said in a group chat that he tried to leverage his position to get a Holocaust denier out of prison. And CNN reported that Collins’ son-in-law has a history of antisemitic statements and white nationalist ties.

A Fox News poll released on July 1 showed Ossoff with 56% support from registered voters, while Collins trailed with 43%. An AARP poll released on Thursday showed Ossoff with a 9 percentage point advantage.

Some Georgia Republicans feel that if Trump becomes more involved, Collins' chances will further erode.

“Collins is gonna get smashed,” Eamon Keegan, a Republican pollster in Georgia, said.

But, Keegan added, Trump's dismal approval ratings would only exacerbate the issue — particularly if the president is unable to resolve the ongoing war in Iran, which continues to drag down Republicans' election prospects.

“One-hundred percent,” said another operative when asked if he believed that Trump could hinder Republican efforts in Georgia.

Trump visited Georgia on Wednesday for an official White House event in Marietta, an Atlanta suburb. Several state and federal officials joined him, including Kelly Loeffler, a former Georgia senator and head of the U.S. Small Business Administration, Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Billed as an official event about Trump savings accounts, much of his speech was about politics, including Collins.

Collins, however, didn't attend. He posted a video to X before the event, saying he needed to be in Washington for House votes, and he knew “the president and the great leaders of Georgia could hold the line today until I get back home.”

During his speech, Trump gave an extended shout-out to Collins.

“Maybe the most important man in this room right now is not here. His name is Mike Collins, and he’s going to beat Pee-wee Herman,” Trump said, referring to Ossoff.

“I said, ‘Mike, I’m sort of here because of you,’” Trump added. “I said, ‘Mike, if you’re here I’m going to be extremely upset with you.’ Because he has to vote.”

Sam Densmore, deputy communications director for Collins’ campaign, disputed in a statement that Collins’ campaign is in tenuous territory.

“[Collins] is going to win this race because he has the business background, bipartisan record of results and positive vision to make life more affordable, safer, and better off for every person in this state, while Jon Ossoff has never had a real job, has gotten nothing accomplished and has a radical voting record,” Densmore said.

The RNC and White House also disputed that Trump could hinder Collins.

“Democrats can spin all the fake narratives they want, but Georgia is President Trump country, and Jon Ossoff’s days in the Senate are numbered,” RNC spokesperson Emma Hall told NOTUS in a statement that targeted Ossoff’s voting record in the Senate.

White House spokesperson Olivia Wales called the president “the Republicans’ best messenger and motivator” to contrast his agenda with congressional Democrats’.

Trump’s focus on the Georgia Senate race was welcome to Democrats and the Ossoff campaign.

“If they could bring back Trump every week, we’d love it,” David Brand, a Georgia Democratic operative supporting the Ossoff campaign, told NOTUS.

The Ossoff campaign has sought to amplify Collins’ relationship with Trump, with ads that feature Trump using Collins’ name at rallies and events over the years. Collins has aligned himself closely with Trump during his time in the House.

“We welcome anything that brings Mike Collins out of hiding and forces him to address his latest scandal, including visits from an increasingly unpopular president who has driven up costs and cut access to health care with the help of his puppet, MAGA loyalist Mike Collins,” Valeria Rivadeneira-Crandell, an Ossoff campaign spokesperson, said in a statement.

The counterargument among Republicans is that Trump’s knack for drawing low-propensity voters to the polls could provide a needed boost to Collins’ chances.

The first Republican operative also said that Collins could benefit from the president’s ability to stoke the MAGA voting base. Trump carried a significant advantage with low-propensity Republican voters in Georgia in 2024, particularly in rural areas. That advantage is harder to calculate compared to his poll numbers before Election Day, but it paid dividends in battleground states for him and his party in 2024.

While he is not on the ballot in 2026, operatives hope his visible support for Collins in the state could still bolster turnout.

“But Collins is going to wear the negative of it as well,” the first Republican operative said.

During the Marietta event, the president avoided the topic that makes Georgia operatives sweat most: complaints about election integrity. Just last week, the president made a prime-time address on the topic — a speech that Georgia Republican operatives were relieved didn’t specifically mention their state — while his dedication to passing the SAVE America Act, a voter-ID bill, has derailed congressional Republicans’ agenda this year.

Georgia has frequently been at the epicenter of Trump’s attacks on elections. After former President Joe Biden’s narrow victory in the state in 2020, Trump demanded that Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger find him additional votes to flip the outcome.

“Those issues are definitely net negatives for Republicans in the state,” the first Republican operative said. “A general election electorate doesn’t have much patience for that.”

Other Georgia Republicans feel it shouldn't be overanalyzed. He's the president, his supporters are incredibly loyal, and his words and presence have wooed middle of the road people before, they argue. One Republican member of the Georgia congressional delegation said as much — with an essential caveat.

“If he stays on message,” the Republican member said, then asked of the Marietta speech: “Did he?”

entries.title: FDA Advisers With Ties to the Peptide Industry Recommend Unapproved Peptides
entries.summary: Pro-peptide appointees by the health secretary are at odds with FDA scientists who say peptides need more study.
entries.content:
A panel of advisers partially appointed by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is recommending the government expand access to six peptides not approved by the Food and Drug Administration.

If the FDA accepts the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee’s recommendations — which is at odds with recommendations by its own scientists — select pharmacies could start using these typically gray-market substances in the specialized medications they create for customers, something that is currently illegal.

An FDA spokesperson said Friday that the agency “appreciates” the panel’s recommendations and will propose a rule the public can comment on, but didn’t provide a timeline. The FDA doesn’t have to accept the panel’s recommendations but it usually does.

Peptides, which are typically injected, are chains of amino acids that serve as the building blocks of protein. Some peptides, including insulin and GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, have been heavily studied and approved by the FDA for years.

The peptides the panel recommended are currently marketed for ulcerative colitis, migraines, pain, wound healing, anti-aging, memory and stroke recovery.

Kennedy, who is a fan of the injections touted by online wellness influencers for a range of health benefits, appointed eight of the panel’s 19 members, all of whom voted to expand access to peptides. Six of those members run clinics that sell peptides.

The meeting over Thursday and Friday attracted unusual attention as the latest illustration of tension between the ballooning wellness industry — which largely views Kennedy as an ally — and government scientists and mainstream medical experts who tend to be more wary of products not approved by the FDA.

“The committee weighed the evidence, followed the science and stood up for medical freedom,” said Lee Rosebush, chair of the American Academy of Peptide Medicine.

The panel did vote 7-6 against recommending one peptide, emideltide, which is believed to promote sleep.

An FDA official said the agency was recommending against the peptide due to “a lack of data to support safety in these substances when used in humans.” FDA officials also recommended against approving the other peptides, stressing they haven’t been studied enough.

That concern was echoed by panel members who voted against recommending the peptides. One member, Todd Durham, cited “low-quality evidence around efficacy and the fact there are approved medical therapies for all the proposed uses.”

But Kennedy appointees who sell peptides stressed anecdotal evidence that they’re beneficial.

“There’s been a mismatch in real-world data versus evidence,” said Gabriel Alizaidy, who works for a telehealth company that sells growth-hormone peptides.

A broad array of other peptides without FDA approval are booming in the United States, promoted by social media influencers touting a broad range of health benefits including speeding healing, improving skin or boosting athletic performance.

Kennedy told podcaster Joe Rogan in February that he was “very anxious” to make peptides more accessible to people from ethical suppliers.

“I’ve used peptides myself and used them to really good effect on a couple of injuries,” Kennedy said.

Access to the six peptides would dramatically expand if the FDA approves them for use by compounding pharmacies, which create customized medications on-site by mixing raw ingredients to fit a specific patient’s health needs.

People often buy unapproved peptides from vendors who label them “for research use only” or websites that source from China, creating safety concerns peptide advocates say could be alleviated by adding them to the list of substances U.S. compounding pharmacies can use.

The American Medical Association has said unapproved peptides should undergo regulatory review by the FDA and third-party testing “to demonstrate their safety and efficacy before marketing or clinical use."

entries.title: South Carolina Keeps the Top Spot on the 2028 Calendar
entries.summary: The DNC narrowly voted to make it first over Nevada.
entries.content:
South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia — that’s the 2028 Democratic presidential primary lineup.

Members of the Democratic National Committee’s Rules and Bylaws panel voted Friday on its presidential nominating calendar, adding two additional states and preserving South Carolina’s first-in-the-nation status. The slate will now go to the DNC’s August meeting for ratification.

The decision comes after days of last-minute negotiations and lobbying, as members privately debated the slate into the wee hours of Friday morning before their public meeting. The early-state selections will shape how presidential campaigns define their own strategies in 2028, ahead of a wide-open and likely crowded primary contest.

“Now, instead of reacting to whomever's left, we now get to shape what the field actually looks like, and I think that's important,” said Jaime Harrison, a former DNC chair and South Carolina Democratic Party chair. “It’s a different role for us.”

South Carolina narrowly edged out Nevada for the first-place slot, after several impassioned speeches by boosters from both states. New Hampshire, which lost its first-in-the-nation primary status in 2022, was a distant third.

It’s not clear how New Hampshire will respond to the new calendar, given that its state law requires it to host the first-in-the-nation primary. In a statement after the vote, the New Hampshire Democratic Party reiterated that the DNC’s decision “does not change the realities governing New Hampshire’s primary, which are beyond the control of both this committee and our state party.”

Several DNC members suggested New Hampshire could hold a party-run primary process, separate from its state-run primary. But it’s not clear whether New Hampshire Democrats would agree to that suggestion.

“Among other issues, it would cost millions of dollars,” said one New Hampshire Democratic operative. “Is the DNC with all of their cash reserves going to pay for that?”

The state’s delegation released a blistering statement, which said the DNC’s decision “is wrong for Democrats, wrong for New Hampshire, and wrong for the country.”

When pressed by reporters on how the DNC would respond to New Hampshire, should state Democrats opt to ignore the DNC’s schedule, DNC Chair Ken Martin said they’d “have to cross that bridge when we get there,” adding that “we don't want to presume anything at this point” about how the state might respond.

Martin went on to cite the tougher sanctions.

“We laid the marker down. This is a calendar this party is actually going to protect. And unlike the past, it’s not going to be a wink and a nod, 'we’ll let you do what you want and you can get away with it,’” Martin said. “If they decided to do that, they know what the consequences are and we’ve been very clear.”

By adding New Mexico and Virginia, the DNC is opening its early window even wider, further diversifying the regions and racial makeups of the states at the front of the contest. Nearly two decades ago, ahead of the 2008 presidential primary, the committee added Nevada and South Carolina to the opening lineup in efforts to highlight the voices of more voters of color.

Martin strongly supported the expansion, urging members on Thursday to add a fifth state that "needs to be from the South."

It was only four years ago that Democrats upended their process ahead of the 2024 election. Then-President Joe Biden elevated South Carolina and pushed to eliminate Iowa, after its disastrous 2020 caucuses. New Hampshire ran an unsanctioned primary in 2024, though the DNC stiffened its penalties on states and candidates that would participate in rogue contests in 2028.

Now, South Carolina will lead off the 2028 primary on Jan. 22, followed by Nevada on Feb. 1. The DNC scheduled New Hampshire for Feb. 8, though it’s not clear if it will follow that guidance. New Mexico would hold its primary on Feb. 15, followed by Michigan on Feb. 22 and Virginia on Feb. 29. Super Tuesday is March 7.

South Carolina’s hold on the influential, first-place perch, as well as additional Southern representation, gained greater salience after the Supreme Court further gutted the Voting Rights Act earlier this year, several members said.

Christale Spain, South Carolina’s Democratic Party chair, said her state provides “the most reliable read" on Black voter "sentiment."

“The South is not the past, it is the future,” she added.

There was some disagreement among members over scheduling New Mexico ahead of Michigan, skipping the midwestern region. But given the speed at which states needed to move their dates, it’s unlikely Michigan could have changed its date, given a Republican-controlled state House.

“Over the period of six weeks, every one of those states is going to get a lot of attention, and so, I don't think it matters where Michigan fell in that calendar, although I understand the concern,” Martin said. “When you think of all the other states and the number of delegates that will come out of Michigan and Virginia, compared to the other states, there's no way they're going to be overlooked by the process.”

Michigan Rep. Debbie Dingell said she’d back the calendar because she wanted to leave the meeting “united.”

"What we are doing this time is building, as we vote for six states, building the story of the Democratic tent," Dingell said. “No one state should ever have a lock on going first."

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

entries.title: U.S. Firefighting Resources Are Already Maxed Out — And It’s Only July
entries.summary: National wildfire response coordinators are triaging across fires raging primarily in Oregon, Colorado and Washington.
entries.content:
The United States does not currently have enough resources to fight every wildfire with a full force.

The country is using nearly all of its wildfire fighting resources far earlier in the season than usual, according to data from the National Interagency Fire Center. On July 18, the country reached “Preparedness Level 5” status, the highest possible level on a scale that measures how much wildfires are taxing resources.

National wildfire response coordinators are currently deciding how resources are deployed across fires raging primarily in Oregon, Colorado and Washington. If another especially big fire starts while resources remain strapped, federal coordinators will have to decide which ongoing and smaller fires will need to be handled with fewer resources.

Since 2010, the United States has only reached a 5 out of 5 on the preparedness level scale by July 18th two other times — 2021 and 2024. Usually, if the country reaches PL5 at all, it happens sometime in August.

Under PL5, national coordinators are forced to make decisions about which fires most deserve hotshot crews, engines, aircraft and other specialized equipment and teams.

“Not every fire that's ongoing is going to get everything that they need to be able to fight the fire and contain the fire,” said one Forest Service official who was granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. “There's a lot of hard decisions that are going to be made as far as allocating resources.”

The fire season has been growing longer in recent years in the United States, stretching from May to November.

This year, there are two main reasons for the resource constraints. Perhaps most critically, limited snowpack and extreme drought conditions in the West have primed the landscape for an early, aggressive start to the fire season.

Second, wildland firefighters have been warning for years that the United States has not properly invested in the firefighters and equipment needed to adequately combat fires during increasingly bad seasons. The Trump administration exacerbated staffing issues when it made cuts to support staff across the federal government, a second firefighting Forest Service official told NOTUS.

“It's both. It truly is. It is declining capacity combined with a continuation of the trend in fire behavior that we're seeing,” this person said.

“As we get into August, certainly September, especially with the activity that we're seeing now, we’ll have to pay attention to just the fatigue that's going to be in the system, and the health of the people that are out,” said the first Forest Service official.

The U.S. Wildland Fire Service did not respond to a request for comment.

“Reaching PL5 earlier than usual increases pressure on national resources, but the incident response system is built for these conditions and is operating as intended," a spokesperson for the U.S. Forest Service told NOTUS. "We use longstanding interagency processes to prioritize the highest-risk incidents and move resources around the country efficiently to where they are needed most.”

New Zealand and Australia are currently sending firefighting resources to the United States to help in the most needed areas, a partnership frequently invoked during PL5 status. The Air Force and the Wyoming and California National Guards have also been called upon to help, sending aircraft and personnel to southern Oregon and northern California.

While Canada and the U.S. often share resources, the same two officials within the Forest Service told NOTUS that is unlikely at the moment because Canada is battling its own severe fires.

Even the extra assistance doesn’t completely alleviate firefighters’ needs.

“When it gets to PL5, I know it’s going to be tough. I know it’s going to be tougher getting fighters to my fire,” said Bobbie Scopa, a retired wildland firefighter who used to manage fire response in Oregon. “You just know that you’re going to have to make tough decisions.”

Oregon has already seen more acres burn this year than the total for the entirety of last year’s fire season. Thousands of lightning strikes from powerful thunderstorms have been starting dozens of fires across the state. More than 1,000 firefighting personnel spent the last week battling an especially large fire still threatening the 4,000-person town of Sisters, Oregon.

Even so, fire experts said that they are more concerned about what could be coming down the pike in the next month or two. California has so far escaped the massive, out-of-control fires that usually characterize an especially bad year.

Scopa worries about what happens if that changes.

“All you need is a couple of days with high winds and some sunny skies and that uncontained fire line does have the potential to get up and run,” she said.

entries.title: The Pentagon Faces Questions After Casualties Disappeared From Public Tracker
entries.summary: The number of service members listed as casualties of the Iran war dropped from 18 soldiers on Wednesday to 14 overnight.
entries.content:
The Department of Defense removed four deceased U.S. service members from its public casualty tracker for the Iran conflict overnight, lowering the number of publicly listed fatalities.

The removal, first reported by The New York Times, lowered the Pentagon’s reported count of U.S. service members killed in the Iran conflict from 18 on Wednesday to 14 on Thursday.

The Defense Department attributed the removal to “temporary data disruptions on the Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) website” on DAY, though the 14 casualties figure remains on the site. But sources told the Times that the Trump administration decided to remove the last four casualties “because their deaths occurred after President Trump declared a ceasefire in the war in April.”

The Defense Casualty Analysis System, a public Pentagon database intended to provide an official accounting of military casualties, is used by journalists, researchers and the public to track the human toll of U.S. conflicts. The unexplained revisions raise questions about the agency’s official public accounting of the war’s death toll.

Asked about the removal, the White House referred NOTUS to the Department of Defense, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Online though, senior administration officials have denied the soldiers were purposely removed.

“This is one of the worst instances of the Fake News media manufacturing lies out of thin air for absolutely no reason at all but to cause distress among the American people,” Sean Parnell, who serves as chief Pentagon spokesperson and assistant to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, posted on X. 

The four service members removed from the list were killed during the latest round of hostilities in the region, including 25-year-old 1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan of Hawaii, 28-year-old Sgt. Angel S. Rampersad of New York, and 19-year-old Pvt. Isabella Gonzales of Texas, who were killed in an Iranian ballistic missile attack in Jordan last week.

Thirty-year-old Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton of North Carolina, who died while conducting a controlled demolition of an Iranian one-way attack drone in Iraq, was also removed from the list.

The tracker has also lowered the number of wounded soldiers in combat from 447 to 420.

Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, who serves on the Armed Services Committee, and other Democratic senators sent a letter to Hegseth and other Pentagon officials on Thursday questioning the inconsistencies between the agency’s reported numbers and other official statements. They requested detailed answers by the end of the month, including an exact casualty breakdown and an explanation of the discrepancies.

“Erasing their sacrifices is a disgraceful attempt by this fragile President to minimize the costs of his illegal war,” Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois), a member of the Armed Services Committee, posted on Friday.

entries.title: The LeBron James Sixers Really Could Win It All
entries.summary: NBA superteams rarely work out. Here's why this one might be different.
entries.content:
Superteams in the modern era of the NBA rarely work out. For a litany of reasons — chemistry, coaching, injury — a collection of stars on one team often doesn’t lead to championships.

The Heat did it, sure. The Warriors did it, of course. But for every Heat and Warriors there are many more teamups that end up in failure and dirt being thrown around in the media.

So there’s reason to be reluctant to … king the 76ers as next season’s champions simply because LeBron James decided on Friday his “last decision” was to sign with them.

But sometimes in basketball the obvious is in front of you. Of course we all should have assumed the Knicks would win the Finals after they kept blowing out all of their Eastern Conference playoff opponents. Of course Victor Wembanyama was going to live up to the hype; he did this before even making it to the NBA.

LeBron James — the LeBron James — just joined a team with former MVP Joel Embiid, former Finals MVP Jaylen Brown and two of the more promising young guards in the NBA in Tyrese Maxey and V. J. Edgecombe.

What weaknesses does this collection of players have?

All five of them are capable of regularly putting up 20 points. Four can regularly give you 30. Three can easily get you 40 or 50 if you absolutely need them to. Oh, and Embiid went for 70 just two years ago.

The 76ers’ defense wasn’t great last season (16th in defensive efficiency) but adding Brown to play alongside Edgecombe on the wing and Embiid in the post makes that unit difficult to score on. James isn’t the all-defensive team player he used to be, but he’s who you fear like Michael Myers lurking on a fastbreak layup attempt.

The bench lacked scoring (32.4 points per game ranked 27th) but the additions of Dean Wade (5.8 points per game) and Anfernee Simons (14.3) should be enough to hold the second unit afloat.

Sure, there’s only one basketball: Brown (3rd) and Embiid (6th) were top 10 in the NBA in usage rate last season; Maxey ranked 27th and James 47th. But when these starting five are on the court you can’t double-team anyone, you can’t sag off of anyone, you can’t zone your way out of those problems. How many lineups in the league have five players who could reasonably take the last shot in a game? I’ll wait.

The one thing that can trip these 76ers up is all the testosterone in that locker room. We know James brings a media circus wherever he sets up, not to mention his style of leadership has at times been described as passive-aggressive. Embiid has no problem throwing a teammate under the bus, as he infamously did to Ben Simmons after the 2021 playoffs. Brown has publicly bad-mouthed Embiid (“[He] flops. He know it.”) and James’ son (“I don't think Bronny is a pro.”) and overall isn’t afraid to say what’s on his mind. Maxey and Edgecomb may not say as much, but their collective demeanors read: Try me if you want to.

Egos or toxicity ruined the 2003-04 and 2012-13 Lakers, the late 2000s Celtics, the 2017-18 Cavaliers, the 2021-22 Nets, and Kevin Durant’s recent stints with the Suns and Rockets.

But if no issues arise in the Philadelphia locker room, and if — big if — Embiid is playing healthy ball in April and May next year, this very well could be the year the 76ers finally do it. (And the fact that they built this team not from intentionally losing games to get high draft picks, as they did in the Process era, is certainly not lost on most Philly fans.) We could be looking at the 2026-27 NBA champions being formed in real time.
